knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Function Over Curve Expressed as a Function of Y

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}6 y\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y + 2$ from $(4,1)$ to $(6,2).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2 t + 2.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2 t + 2,\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=6 y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6 t \\  & =6 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}6 y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left(6 t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}6 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t & =\left[3 \sqrt{5} t^{2}\right]_{1}^{2} \\  & =6 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{2^2}{2}-\frac{1^2}{2}\right) \\  & =6 \sqrt{5}\left(2-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\  & =9 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: regular nonnegative-y curve; increasing endpoint y; scalar arc length

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}2 y\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 y + 1$ from $(5,2)$ to $(11,5).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2 t + 1.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2 t + 1,\,t⟩,\,2\le t\le 5
$$

Note that the domain $2\le t\le 5$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 t + 1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 t \\  & =2 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{2}^{5}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}\left(2 t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{5}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}2 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}2 \sqrt{5} t\,\text{d}t & =\left[\sqrt{5} t^{2}\right]_{2}^{5} \\  & =2 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{5^2}{2}-\frac{2^2}{2}\right) \\  & =2 \sqrt{5}\left(\frac{25}{2}-2\right) \\  & =21 \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

${\int }_{C}8 y\,\text{d}s,$

$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/ca/ca91ec7d1e638b49ab7d4334397c5c7d383b7df0bce022c0e481b857ae2e1b95.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=y^{2}$ from $(1,1)$ to $(12,2 \sqrt{3}),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=t^{2}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨t^{2},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2 \sqrt{3}
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2 \sqrt{3}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t^{2})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2 t\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2 t)^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{6 x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{6 \left(t^{2}\right)}{t} \\  & =6 t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2 \sqrt{3}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2 \sqrt{3}}\left(6 t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2 \sqrt{3}}6 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4 t^{2} + 1,$ $\text{d}u=8 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2 \sqrt{3}}6 t \sqrt{4 t^{2} + 1}\,\text{d}t & =6{\int }_{5}^{49}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{49}\frac{3 \sqrt{u}}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{3}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{49} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2}\right]_{5}^{49} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(49\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{343}{2}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{343}{2} - \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
![](images/c3/c3f6e03956e6002db05950b10d9608be87dd45a4bb75b3822e1ab754981eb19d.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}2 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=\frac{1}{y}$ from $(1,1)$ to $(\frac{1}{2},2),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{1}{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{1}{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 2
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 2$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =- \frac{1}{t^{2}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(- \frac{1}{t^{2}})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{t^{4}}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{4}}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 x y^{6},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 \left(\frac{1}{t}\right) t^{6} \\  & =2 t^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 x y^{6}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\left(2 t^{5}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{4}}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{4} + 1,$ $\text{d}u=4 t^{3}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}2 t^{3} \sqrt{t^{4} + 1}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{2}^{17}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{17}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{2}^{17} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{2}^{17} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(17\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(2\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{17 \sqrt{17}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} + \frac{17 \sqrt{17}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $y^2=6x$ from $(\frac{7}{6},\sqrt{7})$ to $(\frac{8}{3},4).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve can be expressed in the form $x=x(y),$ as follows:

$$
y^2=6x\,⟹\,x=\frac{y^{2}}{6}.
$$

Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=\frac{t^{2}}{6}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨\frac{t^{2}}{6},\,t⟩,\,\sqrt{7}\le t\le 4
$$

Note that the domain $\sqrt{7}\le t\le 4$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t^{2}}{6})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{t}{3}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{t}{3})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=\frac{6 x}{y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{6 \left(\frac{t^{2}}{6}\right)}{t} \\  & =t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{6 x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\left(t\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{t^{2}}{9} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=t^{2} + 9,$ $\text{d}u=2 t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\sqrt{7}}^{4}\frac{t \sqrt{t^{2} + 9}}{3}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{16}^{25}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{16}^{25}\frac{\sqrt{u}}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{16}^{25} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right]_{16}^{25} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(25\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(16\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{9}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{125}{9}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{64}{9}\right)\right) \\  & =\frac{61}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=e^{\frac{y}{2}}$ from $(1,0)$ to $(\sqrt{2},\ln{\left(2 \right)}).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=e^{\frac{t}{2}}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨e^{\frac{t}{2}},\,t⟩,\,0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}
$$

Note that the domain $0\le t\le \ln{\left(2 \right)}$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e^{\frac{t}{2}})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{e^{\frac{t}{2}}}{2})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y},$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2 \left(e^{\frac{t}{2}}\right)^{6} e^{- 2 t} \\  & =2 e^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2 x^{6} e^{- 2 y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\left(2 e^{t}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{\frac{e^{t}}{4} + 1}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=e^{t} + 4,$ $\text{d}u=e^{t}\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}\sqrt{e^{t} + 4} e^{t}\,\text{d}t & =1{\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\cdot\left(1\right)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{5}^{6}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[1\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right]_{5}^{6} \\  & =\left[\frac{2 u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{5}^{6} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(6\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{2 \left(5\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(4 \sqrt{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{10 \sqrt{5}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{10 \sqrt{5}}{3} + 4 \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating the Line Integral of a Function Over Curve Expressed as a Function of Y

question.:question/problem:
![](images/ad/ad80637c8c61ee847bd385c39fb0eec5fc1b14ee4f9d6c1796fb31baff48c016.png)

Evaluate the line integral
${\int }_{C}8 x y\,\text{d}s,$
where $C$ is the section of the curve $x=2 \sqrt{y}$ from $(2,1)$ to $(2 \sqrt{5},5),$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the given curve is of the form $x=x(y),$ Therefore, by setting $y=t,$ we have

$$
x=x(t)=2 \sqrt{t}.
$$

This gives the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
r(t)=⟨2 \sqrt{t},\,t⟩,\,1\le t\le 5
$$

Note that the domain $1\le t\le 5$ is defined by the $y$-coordinates of the end-points on the path.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2 \sqrt{t})i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}})^2+1^2} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{t}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, if  $f(x,y)=8 x y,$ then we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =8 \left(2 \sqrt{t}\right) t \\  & =16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}8 x y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}\left(16 t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)\cdot\left(\sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t}}\right)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{5}16 t \sqrt{t + 1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve this using the substitution $u=4 t + 4,$ $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}16 t \sqrt{t + 1}\,\text{d}t & =8{\int }_{8}^{24}\frac{u-4}{4}\cdot\sqrt{u}\cdot\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{8}^{24}\frac{u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{2} - 2 \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\left[\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{2}{5}u^{5/2}-(4)\cdot\frac{2}{3}u^{3/2}\right)\right]_{8}^{24} \\  & =\left[\frac{u^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5} - \frac{4 u^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right]_{8}^{24} \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{\left(24\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}\right)+\left(- \frac{4 \left(24\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{\left(8\right)^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5}\right)+\left(- \frac{4 \left(8\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =\left(\left(\frac{1152 \sqrt{6}}{5}\right)+\left(- 64 \sqrt{6}\right)\right)-\left(\left(\frac{128 \sqrt{2}}{5}\right)+\left(- \frac{64 \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)\right) \\  & =- \frac{64 \sqrt{2}}{15} + \frac{832 \sqrt{6}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$
